definition: A statement that is either true or false, never both. Propositions are the basic building blocks of propositional logic.
example: "7 is prime" is a true proposition; "Close the door" is not a proposition at all.

definition: The branch of logic that combines whole true/false statements with connectives such as NOT, AND, OR and implies, and works out when the combination is true. It cannot look inside a statement at objects and properties; predicate logic adds that.
example: The guard `if a and not b:` is a propositional formula over a and b.

definition: A letter such as p, q or r that stands for a proposition and so takes the value true or false. It plays the same role as a Boolean variable in code.
example: In p ∧ q, both p and q are propositional variables.

definition: An operator that builds a bigger formula from smaller ones, such as NOT (¬), AND (∧), OR (∨), implies (→) and if and only if (↔). Each connective is defined by its truth table.
example: The connective ∧ joins p and q into p ∧ q, which is true only when both are true.

definition: The connective NOT, written ¬. The negation ¬p is true exactly when p is false.
example: If p is "the cache is up", then ¬p is "the cache is not up".

definition: The connective AND, written ∧. The conjunction p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true.
example: `user.admin and user.verified` is a conjunction.

definition: The connective OR, written ∨. The disjunction p ∨ q is true when at least one of p and q is true, including when both are (inclusive or).
example: p ∨ q is true in three of the four rows of its truth table; only p false and q false makes it false.

definition: The connective "implies", written p → q and read "if p then q". It is false only when p is true and q is false, and says nothing about cause. The implication law says p → q is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q.
example: "If 2 + 2 = 5 then the Moon is cheese" is true as a material conditional, because its premise is false.

definition: The "if" part p of an implication p → q, also called its premise or hypothesis.
example: In "if you pass, I buy dinner", the antecedent is "you pass".

definition: The "then" part q of an implication p → q, also called its conclusion.
example: In "if you pass, I buy dinner", the consequent is "I buy dinner".

definition: The connective "if and only if", written p ↔ q. It is true when p and q have the same truth value, and is equivalent to (p → q) ∧ (q → p): each implies the other.
example: "n is even if and only if n² is even" is a biconditional; proving it needs both directions.

definition: The connective written ⊕: true when exactly one of its two inputs is true. It is the negation of the biconditional, and on Python booleans it is `p != q`.
example: T ⊕ T is false, while T ⊕ F is true.

definition: A table listing every combination of truth values for a formula's variables, one per row, with the formula's value in each. With n variables it has 2 to the power n rows.
example: Two variables need 4 rows; six independent flags need 64.

definition: One of the two values a proposition can take in classical logic: true (T) or false (F).

A conditional or universal statement that is true only because nothing can make it false: its "if" part never holds, or there is nothing to check. An implication with a false premise is vacuously true.
example: Python's `all([])` is `True`: "every element is positive" has no element to break it.

definition: The implication ¬q → ¬p formed from p → q by swapping the two sides and negating both. It is always logically equivalent to the original.
example: The contrapositive of "if it is raining, the ground is wet" is "if the ground is not wet, it is not raining".

definition: The implication q → p formed from p → q by swapping its sides. It is not equivalent to the original in general; assuming it is a classic reasoning error.
example: "If it rains, the ground is wet" does not give "if the ground is wet, it rained": a sprinkler could be on.

definition: The implication ¬p → ¬q formed from p → q by negating both sides. It is equivalent to the converse, not to the original implication.
A formula that is true in every row of its truth table, whatever values its variables take.
example: p ∨ ¬p is a tautology.

definition: A formula that is false in every row of its truth table; more loosely, deriving both a statement and its negation. Reaching one is the goal of a proof by contradiction.
example: p ∧ ¬p is a contradiction.

definition: A formula that is true in some rows of its truth table and false in others: neither a tautology nor a contradiction.
example: p ∧ q is contingent: true when both are true, false otherwise.

definition: A formula is satisfiable if at least one assignment of true/false values to its variables makes it true. Tautologies and contingent formulas are satisfiable; contradictions are not.
example: (x ∨ y) ∧ ¬x is satisfiable with x false and y true.

definition: A formula is unsatisfiable when no assignment of truth values makes it true. A formula is a tautology exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable, which is how SAT solvers prove that something always holds.
example: x ∧ ¬x is unsatisfiable.

definition: Two formulas are logically equivalent, written A ≡ B, when they have the same truth value in every row (every interpretation). Equivalently, A ↔ B is a tautology.
example: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.

definition: The equivalences ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q: to negate an AND, negate each part and switch to OR, and vice versa. The quantifier versions swap ∀ and ∃.
example: `not (a and b)` is the same as `not a or not b`.

definition: The law ¬¬p ≡ p: negating twice gives back the original statement.
example: `not not user.verified` simplifies to `user.verified` for a boolean.

definition: The equivalences p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) and p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r). In logic each of AND and OR distributes over the other. Applying it to reach CNF can make a formula exponentially larger.
The equivalences p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p and p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p: a term is swallowed by a simpler term it contains.
The property that order doesn't matter: p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p and p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p. Logic ignores evaluation order, but short-circuiting code does not.
The property that grouping doesn't matter, as in (p ∧ q) ∧ r ≡ p ∧ (q ∧ r). Implication is not associative, so by convention p → q → r is grouped from the right, as p → (q → r).
The convention for which operator is applied first when there are no brackets. In logic ¬ binds tightest, then ∧, then ∨, then →, then ↔.
example: ¬p ∧ q → r means ((¬p) ∧ q) → r.

definition: A statement assumed as a starting point of an argument, from which the conclusion is drawn. In an implication p → q, p is sometimes also called the premise.
example: In modus ponens the premises are p → q and p, and the conclusion is q.

definition: An argument is valid when its conclusion is true in every situation (every truth-table row, or every interpretation) where all its premises are true. Validity depends only on the form, not on whether the premises are actually true. A single formula is valid when it is true in every interpretation; in propositional logic that means it is a tautology.
example: "If pigs fly I am the Queen; pigs fly; so I am the Queen" is valid, though its premise is false.

definition: An argument that is valid and whose premises are all actually true, so its conclusion must be true.
The valid argument form: from p → q and p, conclude q. Latin for "the way of affirming".
example: If the deploy is faulty the error rate rises; the deploy is faulty; so the error rate rises.

definition: The valid argument form: from p → q and ¬q, conclude ¬p. Latin for "the way of denying"; it is reasoning with the contrapositive.
example: If the cache is down, latency spikes; latency did not spike; so the cache is not down.

definition: The valid argument form: from p → q and q → r, conclude p → r. Implications chain.
The valid argument form: from p ∨ q and ¬p, conclude q. If one of two options is ruled out, the other holds.
Proving a claim by splitting into cases that together cover every possibility and proving it in each one. As an argument form: from p ∨ q, p → r and q → r, conclude r.
example: Every integer is even or odd, so proving a fact about squares for even n and for odd n proves it for all n.

definition: The invalid argument: from p → q and q, conclude p. It assumes the converse; the row p false, q true is a counterexample.
example: "If the cache is down, latency spikes. Latency spiked, so the cache is down." Latency has many causes.

definition: The invalid argument: from p → q and ¬p, conclude ¬q. It assumes the inverse; the row p false, q true is a counterexample.

An argument whose form is invalid, so its conclusion does not follow from its premises even if they are true. (A fallacy in general is any error in reasoning; a formal fallacy is one that lies in the argument's form.)
example: Affirming the consequent is the classic formal fallacy.

definition: In p → q, p is a sufficient condition for q (p alone guarantees q) and q is a necessary condition for p (p cannot happen without q). "p only if q" also means p → q.
example: Having a ticket is necessary for a Friday deploy, not sufficient to force one.

definition: A set of connectives is functionally complete if every possible truth table can be expressed with them alone. {¬, ∧} is complete, and so is NAND on its own.
"Not and", written p ↑ q: false only when both inputs are true. NAND alone can express every truth table, which is why chips can be built from NAND gates only.
example: p ↑ p is ¬p, and (p ↑ q) ↑ (p ↑ q) is p ∧ q.

definition: "Not or": true only when both inputs are false. Like NAND, it is functionally complete on its own.

A circuit element (or, in a formula, a sub-expression) that computes one connective, such as AND, OR, NOT or NAND, from its inputs. Tseitin's transformation gives each gate of a formula its own fresh variable.
A network of logic gates wired together, computing an output from Boolean inputs. Any propositional formula can be drawn as one, and chips are verified by reasoning about them with SAT solvers.
A value that is either true or false, named after George Boole. Python's `True` and `False` are booleans.
Evaluating `and`/`or` left to right and stopping as soon as the result is known. In Python, `x is None or x.size <= 0` never reads `x.size` when x is None.

Solving a problem by trying every candidate, such as every row of a truth table. It is simple and always correct but takes time proportional to the number of candidates, which is 2 to the power n for n variables.
example: Checking 20 variables means about a million rows; 60 variables means over 10^18.

definition: A single case that makes a universal claim false. One counterexample is enough to disprove "for all x, P(x)".
example: n = 40 is a counterexample to "n² + n + 41 is always prime".

definition: A new variable that does not appear anywhere else, introduced to name a sub-formula or to keep an encoding small.
example: Tseitin gives the subformula a ∧ b a fresh variable x with x ↔ (a ∧ b).

definition: A condition checked before running some code, often at the top of a function to return early when the input is unsuitable. Simplifying guards is a daily use of De Morgan's laws.
example: `if x is None or x.size <= 0: return`

definition: A written review after a production incident that records what happened, why, and what will change. Faulty reasoning such as affirming the consequent can lead it to the wrong cause.
A statement with variables that becomes a true-or-false proposition once values are plugged in. It can be seen as a function from values to true/false.
example: Even(x) means "x is even": Even(4) is true and Even(7) is false.

definition: Logic that adds variables ranging over objects, predicates about them, and the quantifiers ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists) to propositional logic. Most mathematics is written in it.
example: "Every admin is verified" is ∀u (Admin(u) → Verified(u)).

definition: The set of allowed values: in logic, the set of things a variable may stand for (the domain of discourse); for a function, the set of inputs it accepts. In logic the domain is part of a statement's meaning: the same formula can be true over one domain and false over another.
example: ∀x ∃y (x · y = 1) is true over the positive reals but false over the integers.

definition: A symbol that says how many values of a variable a statement is about: ∀ ("for all") or ∃ ("there exists").
The quantifier ∀, read "for all": ∀x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for every x in the domain. On a finite domain it is a long AND; over an empty domain it is vacuously true.
example: Python's `all(P(x) for x in D)` computes ∀x P(x) over a finite D.

definition: The quantifier ∃, read "there exists": ∃x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for at least one x in the domain. On a finite domain it is a long OR; over an empty domain it is false.
example: Python's `any(P(x) for x in D)` computes ∃x P(x) over a finite D.

definition: A quantifier over only part of the domain, such as "every admin". The standard shapes are ∀x (A(x) → B(x)) for "every A is B" and ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)) for "some A is B".
A specific value that makes an existential statement true. Proving ∃x P(x) constructively means exhibiting a witness; in Big-O proofs, the chosen constants c and n₀ are witnesses.
example: y = x + 1 is a witness for ∃y (y > x).

definition: Several quantifiers in a row, such as ∀x ∃y. Quantifiers of different kinds cannot be swapped: ∃y ∀x is stronger than ∀x ∃y.
example: "Everyone trusts somebody" (∀x ∃y) differs from "someone is trusted by everyone" (∃y ∀x).

definition: A variable in a formula that no quantifier binds, so its value must come from outside. A formula with free variables is a predicate, not a proposition.
example: In ∀x (x > y), y is free.

definition: A variable that belongs to a quantifier in front of it, like a loop variable. Renaming it consistently to a fresh name changes nothing.
example: In ∀x (x > y), x is bound.

definition: Reusing a name in an inner scope so it hides the same name from an outer scope. It is legal in code and in logic, but confusing.
A database query of the form "find the rows related to every row of another table", such as customers who ordered every product. SQL expresses it with a double NOT EXISTS, using ∀x P ≡ ¬∃x ¬P.
An SQL condition that is true when a subquery returns at least one row: SQL's existential quantifier. NOT EXISTS is true when the subquery returns no rows.
example: Over an empty products table, NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products ...) is true.

definition: Python built-ins: `all(xs)` is True when every item is truthy (and for an empty iterable), and `any(xs)` is True when at least one item is truthy (False for an empty iterable). They are the quantifiers ∀ and ∃ over a finite collection.
example: `all([])` is True and `any([])` is False.

definition: Python syntax that builds a collection or stream from a loop, optionally filtered by `if`, such as `(u.verified for u in users if u.admin)`. The `if` filter plays the role of → in a restricted ∀.
A widely used general-purpose programming language. Its integers have arbitrary precision, and its `and`/`or` short-circuit.
A widely used programming language. Its `int` is a 32-bit signed integer whose arithmetic wraps around on overflow.
Service level objective: a target for how well a service should perform, such as "99.9% of checkout requests finish within 300 ms".
The amount of failure an SLO allows, such as the 0.1% of requests a 99.9% target lets be slow or fail. It is why one slow request does not usually breach a real SLO.
A yes/no problem is undecidable if no algorithm answers it correctly for every input in finite time. Church and Turing showed in 1936 that validity in first-order logic is undecidable.
Gödel's 1929 result that every valid first-order formula has a formal proof. So proofs can be searched for, though the search may never end on a formula that is not valid.
An SMT solver from Microsoft Research, used in program verifiers, symbolic execution tools and policy checkers.
A programming language with built-in verification: you write preconditions, postconditions and loop invariants, and it checks them automatically using an SMT solver.
Notation Θ(g(n)) for a tight growth bound: f grows at the same rate as g, up to constant factors, once n is large enough. It means both O(g(n)) and Big-Omega of g(n).
example: n(n + 1)/2 is Θ(n²).

definition: Notation Ω(g(n)) for an asymptotic lower bound: f grows at least as fast as a constant multiple of g, once n is large enough.
example: Comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

definition: The function written ⌊x⌋ that rounds a number down to the nearest integer.
A chain of justified steps showing a claim holds in every case covered by its assumptions, not just in the cases someone tested.
Proving p → q by assuming p and deriving q step by step from definitions and known facts.
example: Assume m = 2a + 1 and n = 2b + 1; then m + n = 2(a + b + 1), which is even.

definition: Proving p → q by proving its equivalent contrapositive ¬q → ¬p instead: assume q is false and derive that p is false.
example: To show "n² even implies n even", show "n odd implies n² odd".

definition: Proving a statement S by assuming ¬S and deriving something impossible, such as a statement and its negation. Then ¬S must be false, so S is true.
example: The proofs that √2 is irrational and that there are infinitely many primes.

definition: An integer n that can be written as n = 2k for some integer k.
example: 0, 2 and −4 are even.

definition: An integer n that can be written as n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. Every integer is even or odd, and not both.
a divides b, written a ∣ b, when b = a × k for some integer k. Then a is a divisor of b.
A number that can be written as a fraction a/b of integers with b not zero.
example: 0.75 = 3/4 is rational.

definition: A real number that cannot be written as a fraction of two integers.
example: √2 and π are irrational.

definition: The square root of x, written √x, is the non-negative number whose square is x.
An integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Every integer from 2 upwards is a product of primes.
example: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 are prime; 15 = 3 × 5 is not.

definition: An integer greater than 1 that is not prime, so it splits as a product of two smaller integers, each at least 2.
example: 1681 = 41 × 41 is composite.

definition: A whole number, positive, negative or zero: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ….
A counting number. In this module (as in most computer science) the natural numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, …; some books start at 1.
Any number on the continuous number line, including fractions and irrational numbers such as √2 and π.
A smaller proven result used as a stepping stone in a bigger proof, like a tested helper function.
example: The proof that √2 is irrational uses the lemma "if n² is even then n is even".

definition: The theorem that there are infinitely many prime numbers. Euclid's proof multiplies a supposedly complete list of primes and adds 1; the result has a prime factor missing from the list.
example: 2·3·5·7·11·13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509: not prime, but both factors are new primes.

definition: A fraction a/b is in lowest terms when a and b have no common factor other than 1 (their gcd is 1). Any fraction can be reduced to lowest terms.
example: 6/8 in lowest terms is 3/4.

definition: gcd(a, b) is the largest whole number that divides both a and b. Euclid's algorithm computes it.
If more items are put into fewer boxes, some box gets at least two items.
example: Two yes/no comparisons give at most 4 patterns, too few to tell 6 orderings apart.

definition: Covering every possibility. A proof by cases is only valid if its cases are exhaustive; checking every case of a finite domain exhaustively can prove a claim about it.
An existence proof that exhibits a specific object and checks it has the property.
An existence proof that shows something exists without saying which object it is, for example by showing that one of two candidates must work.
example: The proof that irrational a, b exist with a^b rational, via √2^√2.

definition: A proof of a statement of the form "there exists an x with property P". It can be constructive or non-constructive.
A 1934 theorem: if a and b are algebraic numbers, a is not 0 or 1, and b is irrational, then a^b is transcendental, so irrational. It shows √2^√2 is irrational.
An argument that uses the thing it is trying to prove as one of its steps, so it proves nothing.
example: Writing "since n is even" in a proof that n is even.

definition: The polynomial n² + n + 41, noted by Euler, which is prime for n = 0 to 39 but equals 41 × 41 at n = 40: the classic warning that many examples are not a proof.
The problem of deciding, for any program and input, whether the program eventually stops. Turing proved by contradiction that no algorithm can solve it for all cases.
A proven minimum, for example on how many steps any algorithm for a problem must take in the worst case.
example: Any comparison sort needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons for n items.

definition: a mod b is the remainder left after dividing a by b; in Python it is written `a % b`. For b > 0 it is always between 0 and b − 1.
example: 12 mod 5 = 2, and 99 mod 4 = 3.

definition: All the integers that leave the same remainder when divided by a given number.
example: Mod 3, the residue class of 8 is …, 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, ….

definition: A way to prove a claim P(n) for every integer n from some base b: prove P(b) (the base case), then prove that P(n) implies P(n + 1) for an arbitrary n (the inductive step).
example: Proving 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 for all n ≥ 1.

definition: The starting case or cases an induction or recursion is anchored on, proved or computed directly. A step that reaches back k places needs k base cases.
The part of an induction proof that shows, for an arbitrary n, that if the claim holds for n (or all earlier values) it holds for n + 1.
The assumption, made in the inductive step, that the claim holds for the current n (or for all values up to n in strong induction).

Induction where the step may assume the claim for every value from the base up to n, not just n itself. It proves exactly the same things as ordinary induction but is more convenient when the step reaches back further.
example: Proving every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of primes.

definition: Induction over a recursively defined structure such as a list, tree or expression: prove the claim for each base object, then for each construction rule assuming it holds for the parts.
example: Proving every full binary tree has one more leaf than internal nodes.

definition: The fact that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a smallest element. Induction rests on it: a failing case would have a smallest failure, which the step rules out.
Proving a stronger claim than the one wanted, because the stronger inductive hypothesis carries the step when the weaker one gets stuck.
example: Proving S(n) ≤ 2 − 1/n to get S(n) < 2.

definition: A tree data structure in which each node has at most two children.
A binary tree in which every node has either zero or two children. With L leaves it has L − 1 internal nodes, so 2L − 1 nodes in total.
example: A 64-team knockout bracket is a full binary tree with 63 matches.

definition: A node of a tree with no children.
A node of a tree that has at least one child (in a full binary tree, exactly two).
The full binary tree built by Huffman coding, a lossless compression method that gives frequent symbols shorter codes. A tree over 256 symbols has 255 internal nodes.
A competition where each match knocks out the loser. With n teams it has n − 1 matches, because each match eliminates exactly one team.
An equation defining each term of a sequence from earlier terms, such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for merge sort's cost.
A formula that computes a value directly, without recursion or "…".
example: T(n) = n log₂ n + n is a closed form for T(1) = 1, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.

definition: The sequence 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …, where each number is the sum of the two before it: F(n + 1) = F(n) + F(n − 1).
A sorting algorithm that splits the input in half, sorts each half recursively and merges them. It does about n log₂ n comparisons.
The Python exception raised when calls nest deeper than the interpreter's recursion limit (1,000 frames by default in CPython; see sys.getrecursionlimit()).
example: half(1) calling half(−1), half(−3), … never reaches its base case and ends in RecursionError.

definition: A tool, usually part of a compiler, that checks a program uses values consistently with their types before it runs. Proofs that a type system is sound typically use structural induction over the syntax tree.

term: All horses are the same colour
aliases: all horses are the same color
definition: A famous flawed induction proof. Its step assumes two groups of n horses overlap, which fails when going from 1 horse to 2.
The constant π, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159.
example: The sum 1/1² + 1/2² + 1/3² + … approaches π²/6 ≈ 1.645.

definition: log_b(x) is the power b must be raised to to give x. The base-2 logarithm log₂ n is roughly how many times n can be halved before reaching 1.
example: log₂ 8 = 3, because 2³ = 8.

definition: n! is the product 1 × 2 × … × n, the number of ways to order n distinct items. 0! is defined as 1.
example: 3! = 6, so 3 items have 6 orderings.

definition: A statement about a loop's variables that is true every time execution reaches the loop test. Proving it holds initially, is maintained by each iteration, and with the exit condition gives the goal proves the loop correct.
example: For a summing loop: s == sum(a[:i]).

definition: An integer expression that is always at least 0 and strictly decreases on every iteration. Its existence proves the loop terminates, because a non-negative integer cannot decrease forever.
example: hi − lo in binary search; b in Euclid's algorithm.

definition: What should be true after a piece of code runs, such as "s equals the sum of the list".
What must be true before a piece of code runs for its guarantees to apply, such as "the list is sorted".
The guarantee that if the program terminates, its result is correct. It says nothing about whether it terminates.
example: The Collatz loop is partially correct for "x == 1", but nobody can prove it always stops.

definition: Partial correctness plus a proof that the program always terminates.

A system, introduced by Tony Hoare in 1969, for proving programs correct using triples {P} S {Q}: if precondition P holds before S runs and S terminates, postcondition Q holds after. Its rule for while loops is the loop-invariant recipe.
A correctness claim written {P} S {Q}: if P holds before statement S runs, and S terminates, then Q holds afterwards.
Finding a position in a sorted list by repeatedly comparing with the middle element and discarding half of the remaining range. It takes about log₂ n steps.
Python's `bisect.bisect_left(a, x)`: the first index in sorted list a whose element is ≥ x, which is where x would be inserted to keep a sorted.
example: bisect_left([1, 3, 5], 3) is 1.

definition: A bug where a loop or index goes one step too far or stops one step short, very common in binary search.
An ordering in which any two items can be compared and the comparisons are consistent. Binary search needs one; NaN values break it.

A special floating-point value meaning "not a number", such as the result of 0/0. Every ordered comparison (<, ≤, >, ≥) and every == test involving NaN is false (only != is true), so it breaks sorting and searching.
When an arithmetic result is too large for the fixed number of bits in an integer type. Java ints wrap around; in C, signed overflow is undefined behaviour.
What overflowing fixed-width integer arithmetic does in languages such as Java: the result is reduced modulo 2 to the power of the bit width, so going past the maximum lands at large negative values.
A signed integer stored in 32 bits, holding −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (that is, −2³¹ to 2³¹ − 1). Java's `int` is one.
Integer arithmetic whose numbers grow as large as memory allows instead of overflowing. Python integers work this way.
In C and C++, an operation the language standard places no requirements on, such as signed integer overflow. The compiler may assume it never happens, so anything can result.
The Java Development Kit: the compiler, runtime and standard library used to build Java programs. Its `binarySearch` had the famous midpoint overflow bug.
The Java exception thrown when code reads or writes an array position below 0 or at or beyond its length.
The Python exception raised when code reads an attribute an object does not have, such as `x.size` when x is None.
The Python exception for an argument of the right type but an unacceptable value, such as a negative exponent.

Computing x to the power n by squaring the base and halving the exponent each step, multiplying into the result when the exponent is odd. It needs a number of multiplications proportional to log₂ n (at most about 2 × log₂ n) instead of n − 1.
example: 3¹³ takes 4 iterations instead of 12 multiplications.

definition: Computing x to the power n modulo m, usually by repeated squaring with a remainder taken at each step. It is the core operation of RSA.
An attack that learns secrets from how a computation behaves (time taken, power used) rather than its output. Branching on secret exponent bits, as teaching code does, leaks timing.
The algorithm that computes gcd(a, b) by repeatedly replacing (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b is 0; the answer is then a.
A sorting algorithm that grows a sorted prefix one element at a time, shifting larger elements right to insert each new one in place. It takes about n²/2 comparisons in the worst case.
A sorting algorithm that repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and moves it to the end of a sorted prefix, so the prefix always holds the smallest elements overall.
A rearrangement of a collection's items, with nothing added or lost. A correct sort must output a sorted permutation of its input.
A property a data structure's internal state must always satisfy between operations, such as a heap's parent ≤ children. Every public method must restore it before returning.
A property every object of a class must satisfy whenever no method is running, such as an account balance ≥ 0. Constructors establish it and methods preserve it.
A self-balancing binary search tree whose nodes are coloured red or black, with invariants including equal black height (the same number of black nodes on every root-to-leaf path).
A rule the database enforces on its data, such as CHECK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL or foreign-key constraints: data-level invariants.
An SQL constraint requiring a Boolean expression to hold for every row. In PostgreSQL it passes when the expression is TRUE or NULL.
example: CHECK (balance >= 0)

definition: An SQL constraint forbidding two rows with the same value in a column; by default several NULLs are still allowed.
An SQL constraint forbidding NULL in a column.
SQL's marker for a missing or unknown value. Comparisons with NULL give "unknown" rather than true or false.
A database constraint whose check can be postponed until the transaction commits, so it may be temporarily violated inside the transaction.
A specification language by Leslie Lamport for describing concurrent and distributed systems; its model checker explores every reachable state looking for invariant violations.
example: Amazon engineers used it to find subtle bugs in DynamoDB and other services.

definition: Automatically checking that every reachable state of a system model satisfies a property such as an invariant.
Amazon's managed key-value and document database service.
A check in code that a condition holds at that point, failing loudly if not. Python's `assert` statements can be disabled with optimisation (`-O`), so they are not input validation.
example: `assert lo <= hi`

definition: Partitioning an array into three regions (less than, equal to and greater than a pivot) in one pass, maintaining an invariant about the regions. Posed by Edsger Dijkstra.
A sorting algorithm that partitions the array around a pivot and sorts each side recursively. The partition loop is a classic invariant-based algorithm.
The unproved conjecture that repeatedly halving even numbers and replacing odd n with 3n + 1 always reaches 1, for every positive starting integer.
The largest whole number r with r² ≤ n. Python provides it as `math.isqrt`.
example: The integer square root of 10 is 3.

definition: A sorting algorithm that learns about the input only by comparing pairs of elements. Any such algorithm needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons, so Ω(n log n).
The problem of deciding whether some assignment of true/false values makes a propositional formula true. It was the first problem proved NP-complete.
A program that decides SAT for a formula, usually given in CNF, returning a satisfying assignment or a verdict of unsatisfiable. Modern ones use CDCL.
example: MiniSat, Glucose, CaDiCaL and Kissat.

definition: A formula written as an AND of clauses, each clause an OR of literals. It is the standard input format for SAT solvers.
In logic, a variable or its negation, such as x or ¬x.
In CNF, an OR of literals, such as (x ∨ ¬y ∨ z). It is a constraint: at least one of its literals must be true.
A clause with exactly one literal, which forces that literal to be true. During search, a clause with one unassigned literal left and all others false behaves the same way.
example: (¬z) is a unit clause, forcing z false.

definition: A clause with no literals left, which can never be satisfied. Reaching one during propagation is a conflict.

The standard plain-text CNF file format: a header `p cnf <variables> <clauses>`, then clauses as signed integers (−3 means ¬x3) each ended by 0. Named after the Center for Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science.
example: `-2 3 -5 0` is the clause (¬x2 ∨ x3 ∨ ¬x5).

definition: A conversion to CNF that gives each subformula a fresh variable and adds a few clauses defining it, plus a unit clause asserting the output. The result is linear in size and equisatisfiable with the original.
example: x ↔ (a ∧ b) becomes (¬x ∨ a) ∧ (¬x ∨ b) ∧ (x ∨ ¬a ∨ ¬b).

definition: Two formulas are equisatisfiable when one is satisfiable exactly when the other is. They need not be logically equivalent: they may even use different variables.
The number of inputs a gate takes. Bounded fan-in means each gate has at most a fixed number of inputs, so each needs only a constant number of clauses.
Giving each vertex of a graph a colour so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. Deciding whether 3 colours suffice is NP-complete.
example: A triangle can be 3-coloured; K4 cannot.

definition: A graph with an edge between every pair of vertices; Kₙ has n vertices. K4 has 4 vertices and 6 edges.
A node of a graph; edges join pairs of vertices.
A puzzle filling a 9 × 9 grid with digits 1 to 9 so each row, column and 3 × 3 box holds each digit once. As SAT it uses 729 variables, one per cell and digit.
Checking whether a system can reach a bad state within k steps, by encoding k steps of its behaviour as a SAT formula.
The compiler task of assigning a program's variables to the processor's limited registers; it can be modelled as graph colouring.
The class of yes/no problems whose "yes" answers have certificates that can be checked in polynomial time.
example: SAT is in NP: a satisfying assignment is a certificate checked in linear time.

definition: The open question of whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly (NP) can also be solved quickly (P). A fast SAT algorithm would settle it.
Running time bounded by a fixed power of the input size, such as n² or n³. Polynomial-time algorithms are treated as efficient.
Running time (or size) that grows like 2 to the power n or faster, so each extra unit of input multiplies the work.
Running time proportional to the input size.
example: Checking a CNF assignment takes linear time in the number of literals.

definition: A problem whose answer is yes or no, such as "is this formula satisfiable?".
In complexity theory, extra information that lets a "yes" answer be checked quickly, such as a satisfying assignment for SAT.
The 1971 result of Stephen Cook (found independently by Leonid Levin) that SAT is NP-complete: every NP problem can be translated into SAT in polynomial time.
SAT restricted to clauses of at most two literals. It is solvable in linear time using the implication graph.
SAT restricted to clauses of at most three literals. It is already NP-complete.
A clause with at most one positive (un-negated) literal, such as (¬a ∨ ¬b ∨ c), which is the rule (a ∧ b) → c.
SAT restricted to Horn clauses. It is solvable in linear time by propagating forced facts. Dual-Horn (at most one negative literal per clause) is easy too, by flipping every variable.

For 2-SAT, a directed graph with a vertex per literal and, for each clause (a ∨ b), the edges ¬a → b and ¬b → a. The formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some x and ¬x share a strongly connected component.
A maximal set of vertices in a directed graph where every vertex can reach every other by following edges.
A linear-time algorithm that finds all strongly connected components using one depth-first search.
A linear-time algorithm that finds strongly connected components using two depth-first searches, one on the reversed graph.
A logic programming language of facts and Horn-clause rules, evaluated by deriving facts until nothing new appears (a fixed point).
A logic programming language whose programs are Horn clauses, run by backtracking search; unlike finite Datalog, it need not terminate.

The SAT algorithm of Davis, Logemann and Loveland (published 1962), refining the 1960 Davis–Putnam procedure, hence the name DPLL: backtracking search plus unit propagation (and, originally, pure literal elimination).
Search that makes a choice, explores its consequences, and undoes the choice to try another when it hits a dead end.
Repeatedly setting the one remaining literal of any clause whose other literals are all false, since it is forced. One forced value can force others in a chain.
example: With (¬x) and (x ∨ y), unit propagation sets x false and then y true.

definition: If a variable appears with only one polarity (only as x, or only as ¬x), set it to make those literals true; this can only help.
Whether a literal is positive (x) or negative (¬x).
An assignment of true/false values to a formula's variables that makes it true. SAT solvers call it a model.

Conflict-driven clause learning: the algorithm behind modern SAT solvers. It extends DPLL with clause learning, non-chronological backjumping, decision heuristics such as VSIDS, restarts and watched literals.
Adding a new clause, implied by the formula, that rules out a combination of assignments found to cause a conflict, so the solver never repeats it while the clause is kept.
example: Deciding x1 true and x7 false causes a conflict, so learn (¬x1 ∨ x7).

definition: The step in CDCL that traces a conflict back through the propagations to the decisions responsible, producing a learned clause.
Undoing several decisions at once, back to the level where a learned clause first forces a literal, instead of only the most recent decision.

In CDCL conflict analysis, the unique implication point closest to the conflict: a single assignment at the current decision level through which every path to the conflict passes. The standard learning scheme cuts there.
How many decisions (guesses) are in force when an assignment is made. Values forced at level zero hold without any guess; a conflict there means the formula is unsatisfiable.
Variable State Independent Decaying Sum: a decision heuristic that prefers variables involved in recent conflicts, with older activity gradually decaying.
Periodically discarding a SAT solver's current decisions while keeping learned clauses, to escape unlucky early choices.
A propagation data structure: each clause watches two of its literals and is only examined when one of those becomes false, avoiding scans of every clause.
A small, influential open-source CDCL SAT solver by Niklas Eén and Niklas Sörensson.
A CDCL SAT solver derived from MiniSat, known for its learned-clause quality measure.
A modern open-source CDCL SAT solver by Armin Biere.
A high-performance CDCL SAT solver by Armin Biere and colleagues: a reimplementation (port) of CaDiCaL back into C, with improved data structures and scheduling.
An inference rule: from (a ∨ x) and (b ∨ ¬x), derive (a ∨ b). CDCL learned clauses are resolution consequences of the formula.
Deletion Resolution Asymmetric Tautology: a proof-log format SAT solvers emit when they report unsatisfiable, so an independent checker can verify the claim.
A record of a solver's reasoning steps that an independent checker can verify, reducing how much you must trust the solver.
Adding constraints that rule out solutions that are mere relabellings of others (such as swapping colours), to shrink the search.
example: Fixing one vertex to red in an unconstrained colouring problem.

definition: Proving two circuit designs compute the same function, typically by asking a SAT solver whether their outputs can ever differ.
Choosing package versions that satisfy every dependency and conflict constraint. It is NP-complete in general, so package managers often use SAT solvers.
A tool that installs and upgrades software packages and their dependencies, such as DNF, zypper or pip.
An open-source SAT-based dependency solver library used by openSUSE's zypper and Fedora's DNF.
The command-line package manager of openSUSE, built on libsolv.
Fedora's package manager, which resolves dependencies with libsolv.
A Java SAT solver library, used by the Eclipse p2 installer to resolve plug-in dependencies.
The provisioning system that installs and updates Eclipse plug-ins, resolving their dependencies with SAT4J.
Satisfiability Modulo Theories: a solver that extends SAT with richer facts such as integer arithmetic, arrays and bit-vectors. Z3 and cvc5 are examples; Dafny relies on one.
An open-source SMT solver, successor to CVC4.
An AWS tool that uses SMT solvers to reason about IAM access policies, for example to prove a bucket is not publicly accessible.
Identity and Access Management: AWS's service for defining who may perform which actions on which resources, via policies.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing platform.
Running a program on symbolic rather than concrete inputs, collecting path conditions that an SMT solver then solves to find inputs reaching a given branch.
A fixed-width sequence of bits, used by SMT solvers to model machine integers exactly, including overflow.
The number of clauses divided by the number of variables in a formula, used to describe random SAT instances.
Python's immutable set type. The lesson's DPLL code stores each clause as a frozenset of integers.
Logging in with two different kinds of evidence, typically a password plus a one-time code.
A proposed code change submitted for review before it is merged into the main branch.
Continuous integration (CI): automatically building and testing every proposed code change, so a pull request shows whether its tests passed before it is merged.
example: A team rule "merge only if CI passed" blocks pull requests whose automated tests fail.

definition: A runtime switch that turns a feature on or off without redeploying code.

The symbol ⊢, read "proves" or "yields": the formula on its right can be derived from the premises on its left by the rules of a proof system. For classical logic the soundness and completeness theorems make this coincide with semantic consequence (⊨), so this module also uses ⊢ loosely to mean "therefore" (strictly, ∴ is the "therefore" sign).
example: p → q, p ⊢ q is modus ponens.

definition: A ⊨ B means B is true in every interpretation (every truth-table row, or every domain and meaning of the predicates) in which A is true. A ⊭ B means some interpretation makes A true and B false.
example: ∃y ∀x L(x, y) ⊨ ∀x ∃y L(x, y), but not the other way round.

definition: The symbol ∎ (the "tombstone") marks the end of a proof, like the older abbreviation QED, Latin for "which was to be demonstrated".
The symbol ⊬: the conclusion on the right cannot be validly derived from the premises on the left, because some situation makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
example: p → q, q ⊬ p (affirming the consequent).

definition: A loop inside another loop. Its total work is the sum of the inner loop's work over every outer iteration; nested quantifiers such as ∀x ∃y behave like nested loops.
example: An inner loop running i times for i = 1 to n does n(n + 1)/2 iterations in total.

definition: Computer arithmetic on numbers stored with a fixed number of significant binary digits and an exponent. Results are rounded, so rules such as (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) can fail.
A version of a program compiled or run with extra checks (such as assertions) and less optimisation, used during development and testing.
The rule a SAT solver uses to pick which unassigned variable to guess next, and which value to try first. VSIDS is the best-known example.
